title: Salih's warning
hook: the camel is hamstrung, and three days later the cry comes (11:64–68)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hud and his people, the mighty 'Ad, told that asking forgiveness adds strength to strength. Your line was forgiveness is strength. Did you say the sorry you'd been holding? Day four hundred thirty-six.

Every town has one. The bright kid. The one everybody said would go far: the teachers, the neighbors, the aunties at weddings. And then, one day, the bright kid comes home and says something nobody wants to hear. Surah Hud keeps the words Thamud said to their prophet, Salih, and they sound exactly like that town: Salih, you were someone we had real hopes for, before this. You met Salih and the she-camel in al-A'raf. Surah Hud adds what he said before the camel, and what he said after.

Before. Verse sixty-one, in paraphrase: my people, worship God. He brought you out of the earth and settled you in it to build it up. So ask His forgiveness and turn to Him; my Lord is near, and answers. The phrase for settled you is ista'marakum, from the root of 'imara, building, cultivating, making a place live. They are the earth's tenants, not its owners. And God is described not as distant and angry, but as qarib, near, and mujib, the one who answers. Then their reply: we had hopes for you; are you forbidding us what our fathers worshiped? And Salih's answer, in verse sixty-three: if God has given me clear proof and mercy from Himself, who would help me against God if I disobeyed Him? You'd only add to my loss. Then the she-camel of God, a sign: let her graze, don't harm her. And after. They hamstrung her. Salih's last words, in verse sixty-five, are found only in this surah: enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That's a promise that won't be broken. Three days. Not a sudden blow. Three mornings in which a person could still turn, still weep, still ask the God who is near and answers. The surah doesn't say anyone did. On the third, the cry came, and they lay face down in their homes, as if they had never lived there. Salih and those with him were saved by a mercy from God, the verse says, from the disgrace of that day. Mercy was offered three ways: a near God, a gentle animal, and three days of grace. Mercy was the test.
screen: `SETTLED IN THE EARTH TO BUILD IT.` · `MY LORD IS NEAR, AND ANSWERS.` · `WHO WOULD HELP ME AGAINST GOD?` · `THREE DAYS OF GRACE.` · then, large: `MERCY WAS THE TEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a promise to an animal. Sit, and breathe. Think of an animal in your life, or one near it: a pet, a neighbor's dog, the birds at your window, the stray cat by the shop. What does it need from you that it can't ask for? Fresh water, a walk, a little patience, a bowl left out. Picture giving it, and make it a promise you'll keep for the next three days. If you pray, you can thank God for that creature. The bell holds the time.
Salih's warning. In Surah Hud: a God who is near and answers, a she-camel to be left unharmed, and three days of grace after she was hamstrung. Today's word.
Your line: mercy was the test. For the next three days, keep the small promise you made to an animal, and notice how it feels on the third. Day four hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Salih as a lesson about honoring God's signs and showing mercy to animals, and many quote 11:61, 'my Lord is near, and answers,' when encouraging people to ask forgiveness.

original.note: Arabic: "near, answering," Salih's words about God in 11:61.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle animal and a punishment.
what it means: mercy offered three ways, a near God, a gentle animal and three days of grace, and refused.
what a scholar hears: ista'marakum (11:61) is often cited for humanity's role of 'imara, building up the earth; the three-day respite of 11:65 is unique to Surah Hud's telling.

notes: Day 410 (al-A'raf) already told the she-camel, the shared water, al-Hijr and the Nabataean tombs; this day stays with Salih's words in Surah Hud (11:61–66) and refers back.
All Qur'an references paraphrased; confirm the paraphrases of 11:61, 11:62, 11:63, 11:65 and 11:66.
The claim that the three-day respite appears only in Surah Hud's telling: confirm (it is also implied nowhere else in the Thamud passages, to my knowledge).
'Imara as a theological concept drawn from ista'marakum: confirm framing.
